opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so the core challenge with numerical-answer problems is that the formal system doesn't naturally want a number. A theorem prover wants a statement to prove. So the first thing we had to do was turn "find the value of X" into something like "X equals 42," and then prove that. But you don't know it's 42 going in. That's the whole problem.

Under time pressure, the approach split into two tracks running in parallel. One track was the informal side: get the model to reason its way to a candidate answer, often several candidates, the way a strong competition student would. Do the scratch work, try small cases, look for the pattern. The other track was formalization: take the problem statement and write it faithfully in Lean, with the answer left as a slot to fill in.

Then you combine them. You plug in the candidate and try to prove the formal statement. If the proof goes through, you're done, and you have something much stronger than just "the model thinks it's 42." You have a machine-checked guarantee. If it doesn't go through, that's a signal too. Either the candidate is wrong, or the proof is just hard, and part of the skill is telling those apart quickly.

Honestly, the part people underestimate is the statement formalization. If you get the formal statement subtly wrong, an off-by-one in a range, a missing positivity condition, a set that's slightly too big, then you can prove something perfectly and it's still the wrong answer to the actual problem. So we spent a lot of care on that step: cross-checking the formal statement against the natural language, sometimes having independent formalizations and comparing them.

And on time pressure specifically, the mindset was triage. You don't spend equal effort on every problem. Some problems the answer falls out fast and the proof is routine, so you bank those. Others, combinatorics especially, can be brutal to formalize, and you have to decide early how much compute and attention to put there. It's a lot like how a contestant manages a real exam. You don't get stuck on problem three for the whole session.

What I find beautiful about it is that verification changes the game. In a normal competition setting, a confident wrong answer and a confident right answer look the same from the outside. With a prover, they don't. That's really the bet we're making: that verified reasoning is what lets you trust AI on mathematics at all.

r001.rationale: The response describes triaging problems under time pressure, but does not say it prioritized speed over mathematical elegance.

r002.rationale: It says a theorem prover needs a statement to prove, so “find the value of X” must be turned into a claim such as “X equals 42” and proved.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, the first thing we had to confront was that a numerical-answer problem and a proof problem are not the same object, even if they come from the same competition. A proof problem hands you the target: here's the statement, show it's true. A numerical-answer problem hides the target. Nobody tells you the answer is 2025 or 17 or whatever it is. So the prover can't even start proving until something has guessed the number.

So the pipeline we settled on was basically two stages that had to talk to each other. Stage one is generating candidate answers. We'd have the model think informally, compute small cases, look for patterns, run code where it helped, and produce a shortlist. Stage two is formalization: take each candidate, write the statement in Lean as "the answer equals this value," and try to prove it. And the beautiful thing about having a formal checker is that a wrong guess dies very cleanly. If the answer is actually 17 and you conjectured 16, the prover will just never close, or sometimes it will prove the negation outright, which is a very loud signal to move on.

Under time pressure, the real question becomes how you allocate compute between those two stages. If you spend too long enumerating candidates, you starve the prover. If you commit to one candidate too early and it's wrong, you've burned your budget on a dead end. So we did a lot of empirical tuning around that, letting the informal reasoning run until the confidence in a particular value was high enough, then shifting most of the budget to formalizing. And we kept a feedback loop: if the prover got stuck on a candidate, that information went back to the conjecturing side as evidence to rethink.

The other piece that mattered a lot was autoformalization quality. With a numerical problem, a subtle mistranslation is dangerous in a specific way, because you can end up proving a true statement about the wrong problem. So we invested heavily in checking that the formal statement actually captured the competition problem, not just that the proof closed. We'd have the system restate the formalization back in natural language and compare, and we'd reject anything with trivial proofs, because a trivial proof almost always means the statement was vacuous or mis-specified.

And then frankly, a lot of it was just grinding on the test-time behavior. Hours before the deadline, we were watching logs, seeing which problems were stalling and why, adjusting how aggressively the prover backtracked. It's not glamorous. But I think what we learned is that the formal layer is what makes the whole thing safe to do fast. You can afford to be aggressive and speculative on the conjecturing side precisely because the kernel won't let a wrong answer through.

r001.rationale: The response discusses allocating compute under time pressure and shifting from candidate generation to formalization, but does not say speed was prioritized over mathematical elegance.

r002.rationale: It says the prover cannot start proving a numerical-answer problem until a candidate value has been guessed, and describes Lean as the formal proof stage. This communicates that the prover needs an answer supplied before it can prove it.

astra-6.text: I approached it as a translation problem: the original question asked for a number, but for Axiom Prover, we needed a precise statement it could prove. So I separated finding the candidate answer from formalizing and verifying it. Under time pressure, I prioritized problems whose definitions and assumptions could be expressed cleanly, and checked that the formal statement still captured the original question. The key was making sure we were proving the right thing, rather than just getting a proof to go through.

sol-6.1.text:
I approached it by separating two tasks: figuring out the numerical answer and making the reasoning precise enough for Axiom Prover to check. Getting a number is useful, but you still have to establish that it satisfies exactly what the problem asks.

Under time pressure, I’d prioritize problems where the statement could be translated cleanly and where there was a fairly direct proof strategy. I’d try to get one complete example working end to end, then use that to guide the next ones. The key was keeping the feedback loop short—if something failed, was it a problem with the mathematics, the translation, or the proof? That helped me decide where to spend the remaining time.

r001.rationale: The response discusses time pressure and choosing problems with direct proof strategies, but does not say it prioritized getting numerical answers quickly over mathematical elegance.
